Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to find critical regions and critical values for right-tailed hypothesis tests.

Content:
Suppose we have a coin that we suspect is biased towards landing on heads (i.e., the coin is more likely to land on heads than tails). We wish to design a hypothesis test at the [MATH: \alpha = 5\%] significance level to determine whether or not our suspicions are correct with the following null and alternative hypotheses:

Content:
- [MATH: H_0:\:\: p = \dfrac12]
- [MATH: H_1:\:\: p > \dfrac12]

Content:
Let the test statistic [MATH: X] equal the number of heads we get when the coin is tossed at random [MATH: 10] times in a row. Under the null hypothesis, our test statistic [MATH: X] can be modeled as the following binomial random variable:

Content:
[MATH: X\sim B\left(10,\dfrac12\right)]

Content:
The probability mass function [MATH: f(x)] of [MATH: X] is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e078c20d5005ba2883879734dcd3f18b]

Content:
Remember that the critical region contains all [MATH: X]-values that are collectively unlikely under the null hypothesis and, therefore, cause the null hypothesis to be rejected. For right-tailed hypothesis tests, the critical regions lie to the right of the corresponding probability distribution.

Content:
Notice that getting either [MATH: 8,] [MATH: 9,] or [MATH: 10] heads out of [MATH: 10] spins causes us to reject the null hypothesis because

Content:
[MATH: P(X ≥ 8) ≈ 4.4% < α, P(X ≥ 9) ≈ 1.1% < α, P(X ≥ 10) ≈ 0.1% < α.]

Content:
All of these values lie in the critical region. However, [MATH: X=7] does not lie in the critical region because

Content:
[MATH: P(X\geq 7) \approx 11.72\% > \alpha.]

Content:
Therefore, the critical region for this hypothesis test at the [MATH: 5\%] significance level is

Content:
[MATH: X \in \{{\color{red}{8}},9,10\}.]
We can also write this as [MATH: X\geq 8.]

Content:
Finally, [MATH: X={\color{red}{8}}] is the critical value since it lies on the boundary between the critical region and the region where we do not reject [MATH: H_0.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to find critical regions and critical values for right-tailed hypothesis tests.

Content:
Suppose we have a coin that we suspect is biased towards landing on heads (i.e., the coin is more likely to land on heads than tails). We wish to design a hypothesis test at the [MATH: \alpha = 5\%] significance level to determine whether or not our suspicions are correct with the following null and alternative hypotheses:

Content:
- [MATH: H_0:\:\: p = \dfrac12]
- [MATH: H_1:\:\: p > \dfrac12]

Content:
Let the test statistic [MATH: X] equal the number of heads we get when the coin is tossed at random [MATH: 10] times in a row. Under the null hypothesis, our test statistic [MATH: X] can be modeled as the following binomial random variable:

Content:
[MATH: X\sim B\left(10,\dfrac12\right)]

Content:
The probability mass function [MATH: f(x)] of [MATH: X] is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e078c20d5005ba2883879734dcd3f18b]

Content:
Remember that the critical region contains all [MATH: X]-values that are collectively unlikely under the null hypothesis and, therefore, cause the null hypothesis to be rejected. For right-tailed hypothesis tests, the critical regions lie to the right of the corresponding probability distribution.

Content:
Notice that getting either [MATH: 8,] [MATH: 9,] or [MATH: 10] heads out of [MATH: 10] spins causes us to reject the null hypothesis because

Content:
[MATH: P(X ≥ 8) ≈ 4.4% < α, P(X ≥ 9) ≈ 1.1% < α, P(X ≥ 10) ≈ 0.1% < α.]

Content:
All of these values lie in the critical region. However, [MATH: X=7] does not lie in the critical region because

Content:
[MATH: P(X\geq 7) \approx 11.72\% > \alpha.]

Content:
Therefore, the critical region for this hypothesis test at the [MATH: 5\%] significance level is

Content:
[MATH: X \in \{{\color{red}{8}},9,10\}.]
We can also write this as [MATH: X\geq 8.]

Content:
Finally, [MATH: X={\color{red}{8}}] is the critical value since it lies on the boundary between the critical region and the region where we do not reject [MATH: H_0.]
